title: Japan’s Most Dangerous Military Constraint Is Time
gist: U.S. Forces Japan planner Christopher Denzel argues that in a Taiwan contingency the binding constraint on the alliance is time: Japanese legal procedures for access to land, ports and airfields could leave U.S. and Japanese forces undispersed before China's first salvo. Wargames should hunt for 'procedural flexibility' within existing law, as in 2022 and 2023 discoveries that created earlier access paths, to buy Tokyo's cabinet time without presuming its political decisions.

insights.claim: In a 2022 U.S.-Japan wargame, planners believed Japan could grant emergency access to private land for dispersing U.S. forces only after an attack, which would be too late because U.S. forces must disperse before the adversary's first missile salvo.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Base vulnerability to a Chinese first salvo is a core alliance risk; access-law reforms are leading indicators of real readiness for a Taiwan crisis.
insights.quote: the authority’s trigger was also its deadline

insights.claim: Japanese law follows a positive-list approach in which the cabinet can only exercise authorities enumerated in statute, so authorities without implementing procedures may be inaccessible; Articles 76 and 88 of the Self-Defense Forces Act allowed use of force since 1954, but a law on declaring a qualifying contingency only arrived in 2003.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Japan's legalism means procedural reforms, not just budget headlines, determine how fast Japan can act in a crisis.
insights.quote: In the [Self-Defense Forces], when there are no regulations, no action can be taken.

insights.claim: Although the Status of Forces Agreement grants U.S. access to Japanese ports and airfields, most are run by prefectures, municipalities and private companies, and Tokyo lacks a peacetime mechanism to compel access or grant priority to Japanese or American forces.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Civil infrastructure access is a hidden chokepoint; watch for Japanese legislation granting priority use of ports and airfields.

insights.claim: Temporary U.S. use of Japanese land under Article II 4(b) of the Status of Forces Agreement normally takes six months or more in peacetime and requires public disclosure of the plan for use; published estimates range from three to over five months, which U.S. planners in Japan consider optimistic.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Months-long access timelines versus weeks of crisis warning imply the alliance could be caught flat-footed, raising Taiwan-crisis tail risk.
insights.quote: Peacetime implementation can take six months or more and requires public disclosure of the plan for use
insights.locator: Peacetime implementation can take six months

insights.claim: Decades of expeditionary warfare conditioned U.S. planners to assume diplomats deliver access before operations, an assumption that fails in a war fought from Japanese territory where access depends on Japanese political approvals and institutions.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: US war plans built on assumed access may be overly optimistic about early-phase operations in East Asia.

insights.claim: China cannot take Taiwan without impinging on Japanese sovereignty, and Japanese officers argue Beijing could not confidently regard Taiwan as isolated while Japan holds the Sakishima Islands, making them the 'new Fulda Gap' where the first battle of the next war would be fought.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Japan's southwest islands are the likely flashpoint; Japanese defense spending and deployments there are key signals of Taiwan-crisis preparation.

insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Increasing PLA carrier operations east of Taiwan signal rising regional risk relevant to shipping, insurance and Japan/Taiwan equities.

insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Civil evacuation constraints could slow military deployment, extending the period of vulnerability in a crisis.

insights.claim: Planners can develop and rehearse 'procedural flexibility' (room within existing law and process) bilaterally, but cannot credibly script 'political flexibility' (a government's latitude for sovereign decisions); procedural flexibility widens a cabinet's decision window without presuming its choices.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing alliance readiness: watch procedural changes in exercises and white papers, not just political rhetoric.
insights.quote: Planners can develop and rehearse procedural flexibility bilaterally but they cannot credibly script political flexibility.

insights.claim: Japan's record shows strong political flexibility but slow speed: it reinterpreted Article IX, committed in 2022 to 2% of GDP defense spending after a long 1% limit, ended the collective self-defense bar in 2014-2015, adapted Izumo-class ships for F-35Bs, decided in 2022 to acquire counterstrike weapons, and relaxed arms-export restrictions most recently in April 2026.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Japan's steady loosening of defense and export limits supports a multi-year growth story for Japanese defense spending and exports, but crisis-speed decisions remain uncertain.
insights.quote: In the moment of truth, speed may depend more on procedure than on politics.

insights.claim: Planners should assume Tokyo decides as cautiously and as late as its politics allow, and treat that as a design constraint for finding procedural flexibility within stated policy.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Base-case expectation of late Japanese decisions argues for pricing delay risk into any Taiwan-crisis scenario.

insights.claim: In the 2022 wargame a Japanese Ministry of Defense lawyer identified that an 'imminent' armed attack situation, in law since 2003, could provide access authorities without authorizing use of force; the next year's white paper highlighted the distinction and by 2024 it was somewhat routine in exercises.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Shows overlooked legal options can rapidly enter alliance practice, meaning Japan's crisis responsiveness may be faster than conventional wisdom assumes.
insights.locator: The participant who read the law differently

insights.claim: In 2023 a Japanese Ministry of Defense official produced overnight an expedited Article II 4(b) access process meeting legal requirements while preserving operational security; it entered command post exercises in 2024 and was standard play by 2025, though it was never codified.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Uncodified fixes may not hold under real political pressure; codification would be a meaningful readiness signal.

insights.claim: The author argues wargames should include more observers, including policy-level ones, contrary to wargame orthodoxy that limits participants, because institutional problems need institutional reach even at some cost to candor.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Signals evolving alliance planning practices that may improve crisis readiness.

insights.claim: Beijing's sharp reaction to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's November 2025 remarks that a Taiwan crisis could be a survival-threatening situation shows China could read Japanese dispersal in the Sakishimas as preparation for intervention, though such moves might instead deter.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Japanese crisis preparations carry escalation risk with China, relevant to Japan-China trade and market sentiment.

insights.claim: When Washington assumes Tokyo cannot act in a crisis, it presses for advance wartime commitments that Japanese counterparts cannot grant, undermining American credibility and frustrating Japanese counterparts.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Alliance friction over advance commitments is a signal to watch in U.S.-Japan relations.

insights.claim: In a Taiwan contingency, Japanese reinforcements would need to deploy to the Sakishimas, secure off-base access and disperse weeks before the cabinet even considers recognizing an armed attack situation; without procedural flexibility the alliance risks being left with fewer, more escalatory decisions.
insights.speaker: Christopher Denzel
insights.so_what: Without reforms, a Taiwan crisis may escalate faster and more disruptively, a key tail-risk input for Asia exposure.
insights.quote: The Sakishimas are only as defensible as the procedures and authorizations that get forces into position before the first salvo.
